extraction.name: Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD)
extraction.description: A new reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text from the corresponding reading passage.
extraction.creator: Pranav Rajpurkar and Jian Zhang and Konstantin Lopyrev and Percy Liang
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected in three stages: curating passages from Wikipedia, crowdsourcing question-answers on those passages, and obtaining additional answers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia based on internal PageRanks, from which 536 articles were sampled uniformly at random.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Individual paragraphs were extracted from articles, stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions on the content of a paragraph. Questions were entered in a text field, and answers were highlighted in the paragraph.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Daemo platform with Amazon Mechanical Turk
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Additional answers were collected to evaluate human performance and make evaluation more robust. 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one additional crowdworker.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 answers per question in the development and test sets (1 original + at least 2 additional).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers located in the United States or Canada, with a 97% HIT acceptance rate and a minimum of 1000 HITs.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and testing for reading comprehension models.

description.evidence: We present the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), a new reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text from the corresponding reading passage.

url.evidence: The dataset is freely available at https://stanford-qa.com .

creator.evidence: Pranav Rajpurkar and Jian Zhang and Konstantin Lopyrev and Percy Liang

inLanguage.evidence: we used Project Nayuki’s Wikipedia’s internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We collect our dataset in three stages: curating passages, crowdsourcing question-answers on those passages, and obtaining additional answers.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Next, we employed crowdworkers to create questions.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: To retrieve high-quality articles, we used Project Nayuki’s Wikipedia’s internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia, from which we sampled 536 articles uniformly at random.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: From each of these articles, we extracted individual paragraphs, stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: On each paragraph, crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions on the content of that paragraph. The questions had to be entered in a text field, and the answers had to be highlighted in the paragraph.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: We used the Daemo platform (Gaikwad et al., 2015), with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: To get an indication of human performance on SQuAD and to make our evaluation more robust, we obtained at least 2 additional answers for each question in the development and test sets... Over the development and test sets, 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one of the additional crowdworkers.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: we obtained at least 2 additional answers for each question in the development and test sets.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We partitioned the articles randomly into a training set (80%), a development set (10%), and a test set (10%).
